**Verified answer:** The expression diverges to $+\infty$; no finite limit exists.

**Check.** Near $x=2$, write $x=2+t$. Then $\ln(1+t)\approx t$, so $f(x)\approx 1/t$. For $t>0$ this is positive, and $\int_0^\varepsilon dt/t=+\infty$. So $\int_2^{2+\varepsilon} f\,dx=+\infty$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.

The antiderivative $F(x)=-\dfrac{\ln(x-1)}{x-2}+\ln|x-2|-\ln(x-1)$ confirms this. As $\delta\to0^+$, $F(2+\delta)\approx \ln\delta\to-\infty$, so $\int_{2+\delta}^{2+\varepsilon} f\,dx\sim\ln(\varepsilon/\delta)\to+\infty$.

The second term $\int_{3-\varepsilon}^3 f\,dx\to 0$, since $f$ is continuous at $3$. It cannot cancel the divergence at $x=2$.

The supplied program output agrees: the first integral grows without bound as the lower cutoff approaches $2$, and the second term tends to $0$. The claimed value 1 is not supported by any step of the computation.
